new: Winston Smith rewrites yesterday's newspapers for a living, and falls in love anyway. The bleakest thing on the shelf, still quoted in every argument about power, and it offers no way out.
Emma Woodhouse arranges everyone else's marriages with perfect confidence and no self-knowledge whatsoever. Wickedly funny about a comfortable village, and it ends as warmly as you hope.
An American family buys an English manor and refuses to be frightened by the resident spectre, who takes it badly. Ninety-odd pages of impeccable mischief with a surprisingly tender ending.
The livestock throw out the farmer and write their own commandments, then watch the pigs quietly edit them. Short, cold and merciless about how a revolution eats itself. Nobody gets a happy field.

titleAtDraft: The Hobbit; The Lord of the Rings #0
new: Bilbo Baggins is bullied out of his comfortable hole by thirteen dwarves and a wizard with an agenda. Cosy, funny, full of songs, and the doorway to everything Middle-earth becomes later.
Shipwreck by shipwreck, a ship's surgeon washes up among giants, tiny warring courtiers and talking horses. Straight-faced comedy from 1726 that is really a very rude joke about governments.
Two men share rooms on Baker Street, and one of them can read a stranger's whole history off his boots. The case that starts the most famous partnership in crime, with a corpse and no wound.
A Wall Street banker itemises his suits, his business cards and his murders in the same flat voice. Genuinely sickening satire, not for the squeamish, and hard to shake once it is finished.

titleAtDraft: A Good Girl's Guide to Murder
new: Pip picks a five-year-old murder case for her school project, mostly because she refuses to believe the boy everyone blames did it. Interview logs, teenage nerve, and a floor that keeps dropping.

The relatives gather for the will, someone says the old man was murdered, and within a day she is dead too. Poirot sorts the family's polite lies into order, and the answer will annoy you beautifully.
Heat, a pleasure steamer full of grudges, and a honeymoon that ends with a shot in the night. Poirot works through the passenger list while Egypt slides past the windows. Clever, and rather sad.
A wife vanishes on the morning of her fifth anniversary, and her husband keeps saying the wrong thing on camera. Two accounts, one marriage, and the ground shifts hard about halfway through.
Late poems written at four in the morning, brilliant and furious and entirely unwilling to be comforted. Slim, difficult, and the collection that changed what a poem was allowed to sound like.
Liz will put up with the neighbour she cannot stand if it gets her a date with her childhood crush. Romantic comedy logic, a soundtrack running in the margins, and a heart that sneaks up on her.
A house outside Cincinnati is haunted by what slavery did, and by a young woman who turns up at the gate with no past. Ferocious, grief-soaked and not remotely comfortable. Read it slowly.
Kicked out of school again, a sixteen-year-old wanders New York for three days telling you exactly who is a phony and nothing at all about himself. Funny, exhausting, and sadder than it admits.
Two student poets, a married couple who collect them, and email threads sharper than anything anyone says aloud. Cool, precise and quietly devastating about wanting to be chosen.
One Italian summer, a visiting scholar in the spare room, and a seventeen-year-old who notices everything and says nothing. Sun-drunk, aching prose about a season that does not come back.

titleAtDraft: Design Patterns; Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software
authorAtDraft: E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, J. Vlissides
new: Twenty-three recurring solutions to problems every programmer meets twice, named and catalogued so a team can argue in shorthand. Dry as chalk, and still on the desk of everyone who builds software.

titleAtDraft: A Short History of Nearly Everything
new: How big is the universe, how old are the rocks, and which lunatics worked it out? Six hundred pages of cheerful science writing that makes geology sound like very good village gossip.
Twenty years of letters between a broke New York writer and a very correct London bookshop, mostly about secondhand editions and eventually about everything else. Short, wry, and it will get you.
A volunteer's account of the Spanish war from the trenches, and then from the wrong side of a purge. Lice, boredom, courage and betrayal, reported plainly by a man who was shot through the throat.
Acids, explosions and the genuinely disgusting history of chemistry, delivered with cartoons and no dignity whatsoever. Science smuggled in past the gag reflex, and children swallow it whole.

titleAtDraft: Ace; What Asexuality Reveals About Desire, Society and the Meaning of Sex
new: Interviews and reporting on what asexuality actually is, and what a culture assuming everyone wants sex gets wrong about consent, romance and loneliness. Clear, generous and quietly radical.
Seven kingdoms, one throne, and a dozen families willing to spend their children on it. Eight hundred pages of cold politics with dragons at the edges, and nobody is safe for being likeable.
Two human fleets circle a world of spider-like people racing through their own industrial revolution, and only one fleet means them well. Vast, patient, and full of genuinely strange wonder.
An old evil wakes in the high reaches of the galaxy, while two marooned children fall in among sword-carrying pack creatures on a medieval world. Enormous, strange, and worth every page.
Monks of mathematics live behind walls and keep time with clockwork rites, until something appears in the sky and they are sent out. Dense, invented vocabulary, and a puzzle that widens into worlds.
Meg is bad at school, furious, and the only one who can fetch her father back from a planet where every house is identical. Three peculiar old women, a fold in space, and love as the last weapon.
A twelve-year-old criminal mastermind kidnaps a fairy for ransom and learns that the fairies have better weapons than he does. Fast, cheeky, and the opening round of a very long feud.
Five small stories about two amphibian friends: a list of things to do, a garden that refuses to hurry, and a plate of cookies that must be dealt with. Sixty-four pages of perfect gentle nonsense.
An orphan winds the clocks of a Paris station, steals parts for a broken automaton, and stumbles onto a filmmaker everyone forgot. Half the story is told in pencil drawings, and the pages fly.
Five golden tickets, one sweet factory nobody has entered in years, and four children who richly deserve what happens to them. Charlie deserves better, and gets it. Delicious and slightly cruel.
Wilbur the pig has one winter to live, until the spider over his doorway starts writing advertisements for him in her web. Warm, funny barnyard company, and honest about goodbyes.
Three horrible farmers dig up a whole hillside to get at one fox, who simply digs better. Ninety-six pages of thieving, feasting and nerve, with the animals walking off with dinner.
Four cousins, one extremely good dog, and an island with a wrecked ship and a map nobody else has read properly. Picnics, dungeons and villains who never stood a chance. First of many summers.

titleAtDraft: 1,000 Places to See Before You Die
new: Nearly a thousand pages of markets, reefs, hill towns and hotel terraces worth crossing a continent for, each with the practical details attached. Dangerous to leave open near a bank account.
Walking tour of Germany and the Alps, conducted mostly by raft, carriage and any transport that is not walking. Dated in places, still very funny about mountains, opera and the German language.
Australia by train, beer and rented car: a country with a lovely temperament and more creatures that can kill you than anywhere else. Affectionate, funny, and stuffed with alarming history.
A farewell lap around Britain by bus and footpath, arguing with hotel breakfasts and admiring the drizzle. Fond and very rude about the same places, often in the same sentence.
Dictated in a Genoese prison: caravans to the court of the Great Khan, cities of a size Europe refused to believe, and the occasional dragon. Wildly unreliable, and wildly worth the trip.
Two unfit friends set out to walk two thousand miles of the Appalachian Trail with the wrong gear and no plan at all. Bears, snack food, forest history, and a great deal of complaining.

titleAtDraft: Death in Yellowstone; Accidents and Foolhardiness in the First National Park
new: Bears, bison, cliffs and above all the scalding springs: a park historian catalogues every way Yellowstone has killed a visitor, most of them avoidable. Grisly, meticulous, and the best argument ever made for staying on the boardwalk.

titleAtDraft: Women Travel Solo; 30 Inspiring Stories of Adventure, Curiosity and the Power of Self-Discovery
new: Thirty women, thirty solo departures, and thirty accounts of what curiosity does to a person who goes alone. Warm, brisk company for anyone still talking themselves into booking the ticket.

Back roads once printed in blue on old maps carry a man in a van around the whole edge of America, stopping wherever someone will talk. First of a trilogy, and still the measure for slow travel done properly.

titleAtDraft: Elsewhere; One Woman, One Rucksack, One Lifetime of Travel
new: One rucksack, decades of departures, and a reporter's eye for the strangers who turn up when you travel alone. A memoir assembled from single journeys, each carrying its own weight of wonder and loss.

Two great churches, read as the mind of an age: stone, glass and the cult of the Virgin taken as seriously as any philosophy. Dense, rapturous, closer to a long poem about medieval faith than to a guidebook.
Why should a bowl of tea explain a whole civilisation? Because the tearoom holds its art, its manners and its quiet. A slim classic written to show the West what it had been too busy to notice.

Every capital and arch in Venice put on trial, with Gothic craftsmanship acquitted and the Renaissance found guilty of killing the joy of the workman. Learned, opinionated, unhurried; one volume of a larger survey.

titleAtDraft: Bookworm; A Memoir of Childhood Reading
new: Growing up is retold here through the books that did the raising, one shelf at a time. Funny, fond and easy company, the kind of memoir that keeps nudging you towards a reread.

titleAtDraft: Happily Ever After Cookbook; Original Recipes for Book Lovers
new: Recipes built for readers, to be cooked with one hand and a novel propped open under the other. Slim, cheerful and deeply niche: exactly the gift for the friend whose kitchen doubles as a library.

titleAtDraft: Cook As You Are; Recipes for Real Life, Hungry Cooks and Messy Kitchens
new: Cooking for the tired, the broke and the easily overwhelmed, with no lecture about doing it properly. Generous, unfussy recipes and a flat refusal to make anyone feel bad about a messy kitchen.

titleAtDraft: Cook Korean!; A Comic Book with Recipes
new: Kimchi, bibimbap and banchan taught in comic panels, every step drawn rather than described. Bright, funny and unexpectedly practical, whether or not you have cooked Korean food before.

titleAtDraft: A Cook's Tour; Global Adventures in Extreme Cuisines
new: Chasing the perfect meal from Portugal to Vietnam, eating whatever the locals eat and arguing with anyone who calls it extreme. Restless, profane, and better on why people cook than most cookbooks manage.

titleAtDraft: An Age of License; A Travelogue (#1)
new: Drawn on the road: a young cartoonist takes a European book tour and turns the trains, cheese, flirtations and low-grade panic about the future into panels. Light, honest, and first of her travel comics.

Thousands of pages of armies crawling toward each other across two continents, with magic waking in the cold places and nobody safe from one chapter to the next. Epic in the exhausting, blood-soaked sense.

titleAtDraft: Assassin's Apprentice; The Farseer Trilogy Book One
new: Taken in as the king's unacknowledged grandson, a boy is schooled in poisons, politics and a bond with animals nobody at court will admit exists. First of a long apprenticeship in growing up hard.

War splits into a dozen smaller wars, crowns change hands faster than anyone can swear loyalty, and magic keeps creeping in at the edges. Bleak, enormous, and the volume that teaches you not to get attached.

titleAtDraft: Alanna; The First Adventure (The Song of the Lioness #1)
new: Swapping places with her twin, a girl cuts her hair, calls herself Alan and starts the brutal business of page training, unwanted magic gift and all. Brisk, stubborn, and the opening of a knighthood.
Third children are illegal, so Luke lives in an attic and watches the world through a vent, until a face in a neighbour's window changes what hiding costs. Short, tense, best not read before bed.

In a Mississippi town a father answers an unspeakable crime himself, and the lawyer defending him must sell that to a jury while the streets outside pick sides. Ugly, angry, impossible to read neutrally.

Convicted of murder as a servant girl, Grace Marks tells her story to a doctor who wants her mind mapped, and every telling shifts a little. Slippery, patient historical crime that never lets you settle.

Vatican City has hours to live, a stolen canister ticking somewhere beneath it, and a symbologist chasing an old brotherhood's markers across Rome at a dead sprint. Daft, propulsive, paced like a chase.

Behind a diner's pantry lies a door into the past, and the schoolteacher who steps through means to stop an assassination. Long, tender, and shrewd about how hard history shoves back when you shove it.
Newlyweds are being murdered in San Francisco, and the homicide inspector on the case builds her own off-books team of four women to crack it. Short chapters, fast pulse, first of a very long series.

Six teenagers, one stranded motorhome, and a shooter out in the dark who says nobody leaves until a secret gets confessed. One night, told almost in real time, and the friend group will not survive it whole.
Onstage, an aging court composer confesses a lifetime of envy: he alone recognised the giggling, vulgar young genius, and he hated God for the choice. Wickedly funny about being merely competent.
What is left of a warship's mind walks around in a single borrowed body, carrying a grudge against an empire that thinks in centuries. Cold, strange, and quietly furious about who counts as a person.

Barely more than a hundred pages of poems and quiet reflection, fond of weather and open ground, content to sit with a question rather than settle it. Gentle reading for an evening with nowhere to be.
One performer, seven movements, and a grief that belongs to a whole people rather than to one funeral. Australian Indigenous theatre mixing poetry, history and plain fury, all inside eighty pages.

The ghost on the battlements names a murderer, and the prince who hears it thinks himself half to death before he moves. Still the sharpest thing ever written about grief, doubt and the price of delay.

Plague comes to a Warwickshire household, and the mother at its centre, herb-wise and half-feared by her neighbours, cannot keep it from her son. Grief written so closely it aches, with a play waiting after.

Two schoolboys get seated together in form and one of them falls hard, drawn in soft pencil with leaves tumbling across the panels. Sweet, queer, low-stakes comics, and the start of something ongoing.

Every surviving scrap of Sappho, brackets and all, with the gaps left visible so the silence does its share of the work. Desire in fragments, and somehow more devastating for everything that burned away.
Honourable men talk themselves into a knife, then find that killing a ruler was the easy half. Cold, argumentative political theatre, plus the finest funeral speech ever used to turn a crowd.
Money and a door that locks: the two things Woolf says a woman needs before she can write, argued in lectures that wander, joke, then land like a verdict. Slim, and still waiting for a decent answer.
Out on the marshes a decaying manor shelters the last heiress of a cursed line, and the phantom riders of the old legend are already stirring. Belarusian gothic, thick with fog and cleverly plotted.

titleAtDraft: Around the World in Eighty Days
new: An English gentleman bets his fortune that trains and steamers can carry him round the globe on schedule, then sets off with a bewildered French valet. Brisk, funny, and charmingly dated about the world.

titleAtDraft: The Acts of King Arthur and His Noble Knights
new: Malory's knights are turned back into men who sweat, doubt and argue, in a retelling its author never lived to finish. Scholarly, affectionate, and strange in the best way for lovers of the old Arthur.

titleAtDraft: The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn; Adventures of Tom and Huck #2
new: Down the Mississippi on a raft go a runaway boy and a runaway man, dodging frauds, feuds and the boy's own conscience. Funny, uncomfortable, and argued over in classrooms ever since.

titleAtDraft: Five Little Peppers and How They Grew; Five Little Peppers #1
new: Five children and their widowed mother keep a cheerful house on almost nothing, and mend, scheme and sing their way through every setback. Sentimental, cosy, wholly of its century, and first of many.

On a lonely mountain a wizard's daughter keeps company with legendary beasts and wants nothing at all from people, until a baby is left in her arms. Lyrical, fierce, and quietly clear about what vengeance costs.

titleAtDraft: Rosalind Franklin; The Dark Lady of DNA
new: The crystallographer whose images made the double helix possible, and whose credit went elsewhere, gets a careful full-length life here. Science, snobbery and X-ray film, with no rush to sainthood.
Parsing, punctuation and the parts of speech, laid out for schoolrooms two centuries ago in the flattest voice imaginable. Arid, gloriously obsolete, and a treat if you collect such things.
Slim, specialist and unapologetic about it: a mid-century account of one architect's work and the working life behind it. If modern buildings are your thing, here is a quiet afternoon well spent.

Villa by villa through Italy, measuring terraces, cypress walks and water stairs with an eye that cares about proportion rather than pretty flowers. Exacting, unsentimental, and a gardener's dream of an itinerary.

titleAtDraft: Journey to the Centre of the Earth
new: Down a volcano in Iceland go a professor, his reluctant nephew and an unflappable guide, following a coded parchment toward the basement of the world. Wildly unscientific, and wildly good fun.

titleAtDraft: Rambles in Germany and Italy; in 1840, 1842, and 1843
new: Letters home from a widow travelling the continent with her grown son, taking in galleries, lakes, politics and her own long memories. Unhurried, particular, and far more personal than most such journals of its day.
Flower fairies, elves and small moral errands in the woods, written to amuse one child long before her author was famous. Sweet, slight, occasionally preachy, and a curiosity worth the shelf space.
The zookeeper says goodnight, the gorilla lifts his keys, and the whole zoo tiptoes home to bed behind him. Almost wordless, endlessly rereadable, and small children spot the balloon before you do.

Doing the laundry ends with an eleven-year-old and his toddler sister dropping through a grate into a subterranean world of giant bats and warring rats, where a prophecy is waiting with his name in it.

An orphan is handed to a gruff grandfather high in the Alps, thrives among goats and mountain air, then is carried off to a city house that cannot hold her. Warm, old-fashioned, and sure of its happy ending.

Two horrible aunts, a handful of spilled magic, and a peach that grows bigger than a house. Inside it wait a spider, a grasshopper and a centipede, and one lonely boy finally has a family worth sailing off with.

Thirteen is the age a young witch must leave home for a year, so off she flies with a talkative black cat and one useful skill. Setting up a delivery service in a seaside town turns out to be the harder trick.

Grey gentlemen in grey hats are talking a town into saving its time, and only a girl living in a ruined amphitheatre notices what is being stolen. Fable-shaped, with a tortoise who spells out the future.

Two children and an old sailor lift off under a magic umbrella and land clean off the map, on an island split between a blue half and a pink half that cannot abide each other. Sunny, silly nonsense throughout.

The school bus stalls in the fog on the way back from a farm, the scarecrows in the fields have moved, and a stopped watch spells out advice: keep to small spaces. Genuinely frightening, and only the first.

titleAtDraft: The Bad Beginning; (A Series of Unfortunate Events)
new: Three clever orphans, one enormous fortune, and a guardian with a single eyebrow and theatrical ambitions. The narrator warns you off every few pages, which is of course why the next twelve books exist.

titleAtDraft: The Happy Prince and Other Tales
new: Piece by piece, a gilded statue and the swallow who stayed too late in the season give away everything they have. Five short fairy tales, sharp-witted on the surface and quietly heartbreaking underneath.

The pilot dies mid-flight and a thirteen-year-old puts the little plane down in a Canadian lake with nothing useful but the hatchet on his belt. Fire, fish, a moose, and the slow arithmetic of staying alive.

Two elderly sisters report creaking floors, odd music and vanishing valuables in their old mansion, so the teenage detective packs a bag and goes looking for the passage behind it all. Brisk, tidy, vintage.

A shortcut across a construction site puts five kids in front of a dying alien, who hands them the power to become any animal they touch. The parasites already walking among them will not expect a hawk.

Stranded in the desert, a pilot meets a small traveller who has left his planet and his one rose behind and is working his way from world to world. A fox explains love to him, and the ending does not soften it.
Truffula trees fall, smog rises, and a small mossy creature speaks for the trees while nobody listens. Bouncing rhyme and invented words carrying a blunt lesson about what a factory does to a forest.
Hiding in a school attic with a stolen book, a bullied boy finds the world inside it being eaten by Nothing. Long, strange and layered, with a second half about getting every wish you ever asked for.

titleAtDraft: A Place to Hang the Moon
new: Three orphaned siblings are evacuated out of wartime London with a private plan: find not simply a billet but somebody to keep them. Book-loving, warm-hearted, and headed exactly where you hope it is headed.

Dozens of tales gathered from Norse, Russian, Hungarian and Native American sources, with emperors, witches and talking birds among them. One volume of the coloured series that shaped the fairy-tale shelf.

titleAtDraft: Theodora Hendrix and the Curious Case of the Cursed Beetle
new: Monsters, curses and a beetle that plainly should have been left alone. Recent middle-grade spookiness, long enough to last a week of bedtimes, and creepy in the cheerful way rather than the sleepless way.

titleAtDraft: There's A Ghost In This House
new: A girl gives you a tour of her house, certain that a ghost lives somewhere in it, while tracing-paper overlays keep showing exactly what she misses. A picture book that turns page-turning into the joke.
Sent to bed without supper in his wolf suit, a boy sails off to be crowned king of some very toothy monsters. Ten sentences, enormous pictures, and a last page about supper still being warm.

Follow a waistcoated rabbit down a hole and the rules stop applying: a caterpillar on a hookah, a tea party with no end, a queen who sentences first. Nonsense logic, verse and riddles, none of it dated.

titleAtDraft: The Eleventh Hour; A Curious Mystery
new: An elephant throws an eleventh birthday party for eleven animal guests, and someone eats the feast before the clock strikes. Rhyming verse over densely coded pictures, with the solution sealed at the back.

titleAtDraft: How Winston Delivered Christmas; A Christmas Story in Twenty-Four-and-a-Half Chapters
new: One small mouse finds a letter addressed to Father Christmas and decides it simply must be delivered. Twenty-four and a half chapters, one per December day, with crafts and recipes tucked in between them.

Her parents treat reading as a disease and her headmistress throws children by the pigtails, but a small girl with a library card and a peculiar talent behind her eyes evens the score. Wickedly funny revenge.

titleAtDraft: Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children
new: After his grandfather dies raving about monsters, a teenager follows the old photographs to a ruined house on a Welsh island where the same day keeps repeating. Built around genuinely eerie found snapshots.

Before the pirates and the crocodile, Peter was a week-old baby who flew out of the nursery window and settled in among the birds and fairies of a London park. Lyrical, wistful, stranger than the play it became.

His uncle dies in a car crash that was nothing of the kind, and a fourteen-year-old discovers the holiday hobbies he was taught were spy training all along. Gadgets, a billionaire, a first mission. Book one.

titleAtDraft: The House with a Clock in Its Walls
new: The shabby uncle who takes in an orphaned boy turns out to be a wizard, and something ticks inside the plaster of his mansion, counting toward a very bad end. Creaky, gothic, and pitched at nervous readers.

Swallowed by a whirlpool, a girl and her sailor friend wash up on the road to Jinxland, where a nasty king rules and a princess has had her heart frozen. The straw-stuffed hero arrives to sort it out.

Snow overnight, and a boy in a red snowsuit goes out to make tracks, knock the drifts off a tree and save a snowball in his pocket. Collage pictures, very few words, perfect for the smallest listeners.

After the war a teenage girl farms the sheltered valley she believes is the last living place on earth, until smoke shows on the ridge and a stranger in a safe suit walks in. A diary that tightens page by page.

Inside a round tower on a rock, a keeper trims the wick, fills the log and waits out fog and ice while his family grows. Watercolours built for the shape of the page, and a quiet look at work being made obsolete.

titleAtDraft: The Boy, The Mole, The Fox and The Horse; (Book 1)
new: Four unlikely friends wander a bare landscape and talk about kindness, fear and cake. Handwritten lines under ink and watercolour drawings, meant to be opened anywhere rather than read straight through.

Seven magic orbs scattered across the world will summon a dragon who grants a wish. A girl hunting them falls in with a boy who has a monkey tail and startling strength. Slapstick, tournaments, a long run ahead.

Wrongdoing, wisecracks and a caper unfolding a long way from any police station. Light company for one evening, one entry in a longer run, and generous enough to send you off grinning rather than grim.

Pip has closed cases before, and now somebody is posting her taunts that quote one of them. The third turn of a small-town series where the sleuth is the one coming apart, and the bill for asking questions finally arrives.

America's most effective conversion camp boasts a spotless success rate, and Rose is beginning to see what it actually costs. Queer horror with teeth, furious at the institution, and still willing to grant its heroine daylight.

Libby Day survived the night her family was slaughtered and testified against her own brother. Broke and out of sympathy years later, she takes money from murder hobbyists to go back and check. Mean, bleak, unputdownable.

Bored and brilliant, a top student finds a notebook that kills anyone whose name he writes in it, and decides the world needs pruning. First volume of a manga duel between a boy with a god complex and the detective reading his moves.

Sprung from a filthy cell on the condition that she help anyone who asks, a bitter healer and her silent giant of a companion reach a woodland where a prince's bride is not quite who she was. Old Ireland, quiet magic, book one.

Two years without rain, and a farming town buries a family it half believes shot itself. The federal investigator who comes home for the funeral left under a cloud of his own. Dust, grudges, and a whodunnit that keeps its cards.

Four novellas about ordinary people who step over a line and then have to live in the room with it: a farmer, a novelist, a bargain too good to refuse, a wife who finds something in the garage. Plain-spoken, no comfort offered.

Done with detective work and having said so publicly, Pip picks it up again when a friend's brother vanishes and the police shrug. A missing-person hunt told through her podcast, with school, guilt and growing up crowding in.

Her father got rich writing about the house that drove the family out in the night. The house is hers now, she is certain the book was a lie, and she has come back with tools. Chapters of that old bestseller sit between hers.

Ten years served, and the actor walks out ready to tell a retired detective what really happened at the Shakespeare conservatory. Seven fourth-year students, one death, and verse doing the work of confession. Theatrical and doomed.

Two killers, a farmhouse in Holcomb, Kansas, and a family shot in their own beds: the reporting that followed invented a genre. Neighbours, lawmen and the long wait on death row, set down with awful calm. True crime before the term.

Why would a billionaire leave everything to a schoolgirl he never met? To find out she has to live in his mansion with the grandsons he cut off. Riddles in the panelling, four furious heirs, and a series that enjoys withholding.

Derry, Maine eats its children on a schedule, and seven misfits are the only ones who notice. Decades later the phone rings and they go back. Over a thousand pages of friendship, memory, and something wearing a clown suit.

Her twin sister was famous, beloved online, and is now dead on the floor of a spotless apartment. Stepping into that life looks easier than explaining it. Fast, nasty satire of influencer sainthood with a body underneath.

Waking from a crash in a stranger's spare room with his legs ruined, a novelist learns that his rescuer has read everything he ever wrote and hated how the last one ended. Two people, one typewriter, and nobody coming up the road.

Snowdrifts halt the train somewhere in the Balkans, a passenger is found stabbed behind a bolted door, and every traveller in the carriage has a tidy alibi. The Belgian works the corridor. Famous ending, best reached cold.

Five students walk into detention and only four walk out. Each survivor had something the dead boy was about to publish, and the whole school is delighted to speculate. Four narrators, all of them lying about something.

Behind the children's pet graveyard in the Maine woods lies older ground that returns what you bury, not quite as it went in. A father learns this, then finds a reason to use it. Grief written as horror, and merciless with it.

Coaxed out of retirement, a profiler hunts a killer who works through whole families by moonlight, and the only mind that can help belongs to the man who nearly finished him. Empathy as an occupational injury. Where Lecter begins.

A bank robbery goes wrong and the robber ends up holding an apartment viewing hostage, which turns out to be eight strangers who badly needed an excuse to talk. Warm, funny, far more curious about people than about the crime.

titleAtDraft: Bait and Witch; (Witch Way Librarian Mysteries #1)
new: Exiled to a tiny Oregon town after saying the wrong thing in Washington, a librarian discovers the books whisper to her and that someone in the woods has died. Cosy magic, small-town suspicion, and the start of a series.

Ninth-graders wake on an island wearing metal collars, with orders to kill one another until one is left. Forty-two classmates, three days, and a government that files the whole thing as research. Long, brutal, and relentless.

Blackmail is the job a dying general hires the private eye for, and it opens onto every rotten thing his daughters have touched. Los Angeles in the rain, a plot knotted past untying, and sentences worth every bit of the trouble.

Fog, and a lawsuit that has outlived its litigants, while a great lady's past comes up the drive and a police inspector starts asking questions. Vast, furious at the courts, and ancestor to every detective novel written since.

An insult demands payment, and the man who received it has been patient about the arrangements. Carnival overhead, damp catacombs below, a rare sherry promised at the end of the passage. Barely thirty pages of smiling malice.

titleAtDraft: The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time
new: Somebody has killed the neighbour's dog with a garden fork, so the fifteen-year-old who finds it opens an investigation, Holmes-fashion. Prime numbers for chapter headings, and a narrator constitutionally unable to lie.

One year after burying her son, a Las Vegas producer starts finding messages insisting he is not dead. Grief, a cruel hoax, or something worse behind a government fence in the mountains. Brisk, paranoid, built for one sitting.

titleAtDraft: The Fall of the House of Usher
new: Invited to a crumbling house that appears to be ill along with its owner, a visitor finds Roderick Usher nerve-flayed and his sister fading. Dread as architecture, and this edition pads the doom out with more tales and verse.

An ordinary morning ends with her husband named on the news as a hostage-taker, leaving behind a note she cannot read straight. Years of not knowing, a negotiator who never let go, and a reason that keeps shifting shape.

Three girls walked out of their cabin one night at summer camp and never came back. The one left behind has spent fifteen years painting them, and now the camp reopens and she takes the job. Lake, woods, Two Truths and a Lie.

titleAtDraft: The Lighthouse Mystery; The Boxcar Children #8
new: Summer in a cottage beside a working lighthouse, and the Alden children start noticing what the grown-ups have not: odd lights, odd noises, a stray in need of feeding. Tidy, gentle detective work, finished in an afternoon.

Summoned to Washington to give a lecture, the symbologist arrives to find his mentor taken and a Masonic riddle pinned to the ransom. Capitol crypts, a tattooed fanatic, one very long night of chases and impromptu seminars.

Molly cleans hotel suites to a standard nobody asked for, reads people badly, and finds a wealthy guest extremely dead in his bed. Suspicion lands on whoever touched everything. Funny, kind, and a proper puzzle underneath.

The least-liked man in St Mary Mead is shot in the vicar's study, and half the village would take credit. Enter an elderly spinster who gardens, listens, and is never wrong. Village crime's sharpest knitter, making her debut.

titleAtDraft: The Murder of Roger Ackroyd (Hercule Poirot Series)
new: Village gossip about a widow's death turns serious when the squire of King's Abbot is found stabbed behind a locked door. The retired Belgian next door sets down his marrows. The most argued-over solution in crime, and it plays fair.

The mistress of Styles Court dies of strychnine in a house full of relatives who all stood to gain, and the little Belgian refugee in the village turns out to have been a policeman. Where Poirot starts, with the war still on.

titleAtDraft: The Mysterious Benedict Society; The Mysterious Benedict Society #1
new: Answer an odd little newspaper advert, pass some very strange tests, and four gifted children find themselves sent undercover into a boarding school that is broadcasting something at the world. Codes, gadgets and proper villainy.

Winter caretaker at a grand empty hotel sounds like the fresh start a drinking writer needs, and his small son already knows better. Months of snow, a boiler wanting attention, and a building with an appetite for families.

A trainee agent is sent to trade scraps of her own history with a caged psychiatrist, because he may know who is skinning women in the Midwest. Two interrogations running at once, only one of them official. Still the benchmark.

The narrator would like it understood that he is not mad, merely sharp of hearing, and that the old man's clouded eye left him no choice at all. Thirty pages of murder told by the least trustworthy voice in the language.

Midnight on a lonely road, one stranger dressed in white, and an inheritance worth ruining a woman for. Sworn testimonies fit slowly together: Victorian sensation at full pitch, cruel in places and tender in others.

Publishing is a small world, and a stolen manuscript is a very loud secret. Sharp, gossipy, horribly funny satire that keeps twisting the knife about who gets to tell whose story, and who gets paid for it.
Long, dark and deliberately nasty contemporary crime, heavy on dread and worse, for readers who want a mystery that keeps twisting and never once flinches at the ugly parts.

One student vanishes from a Manchester tower block, and the case resurfaces years later as interviews, emails and flat contradictions. Assembled like a real documentary, which is what makes it unsettling.

June inherits the family flower farm and the family affliction: voices, a door nobody else can see, and a mother who disappeared without explanation. Half missing-person case, half love story across time.

titleAtDraft: The Unusual Suspects; The Sisters Grimm #2
new: Two sisters go undercover at a school where the teachers stepped straight out of old fairy tales, one of them now extremely dead and something enormous stirring underground. Funny, fast and crawling with monsters.

titleAtDraft: Vera Wong's Unsolicited Advice for Murderers; Vera Wong #1
new: Vera runs a tea shop nobody visits, finds a dead man on the floor, quietly pockets the evidence and invites the suspects round for oolong. Nosy, bossy and completely delightful cozy sleuthing.
Bodies drained of blood in the Pacific Northwest, killers who believe they are vampires, and a Washington detective who cannot shake the taunts of an old enemy. Grim, quick, built for one sitting.
Two brothers, one rented room, a deck of cards and a hustle neither can quite leave alone. A short, savage, wickedly funny play about money, blood ties and the con that never stops paying.
Cozy crime with a tearoom appetite: light, brisk, gently nosy, and part of a series that treats a killing as something to be sorted out over a warm scone and a very strong pot of tea.

Sick leave gives a Tokyo detective time to look for a relative's missing fiancee, and the trail runs through debt, borrowed names and lives bought secondhand. Japanese crime writing at its quietest and most furious.
Six teenagers, one locked room, a syringe on the table and a note demanding that one of them die before the timer runs down. Sharp teen suspense that keeps cutting back to how they all got invited.
Inquest transcripts, letters and survivor statements circle one small-town catastrophe and the bullied girl at its centre, whose strange power nobody believed in until it was far too late.

titleAtDraft: Case Closed; One and the Same? (Vol. 3)
new: A teenage detective trapped in a child's body keeps cracking cases nobody will let him take credit for. Compact, fairly clued puzzles in comic form, this volume built around a problem of look-alikes.
Yadriel wants his family to accept him as a brujo, so he summons a spirit to prove it and gets the wrong ghost entirely: a loud, charming boy who refuses to move on until his own death is explained.

Chalk figures on the pavement were a private code between friends one long summer, until one of them pointed the way to a body in the woods. Decades later the drawings start again. Nasty, nostalgic, dread-soaked.
Short, shivery tales gathered for one dark evening: a slim collection that prefers atmosphere and unanswered questions to tidy explanations, and can be finished before the candle burns down.
Framed, imprisoned and stripped of everything, Tracy Whitney leaves that cell with a talent for elaborate revenge and a taste for other people's jewels. Big, glossy, propulsive caper storytelling.

Fire gutted the Los Angeles Central Library and the arson case never quite closed. Part investigation, part civic history, part ode to what libraries hold and to the people who would rather they burned.
Eight stage whodunnits in one brick of a book, headed by the snowed-in guesthouse thriller still running in London. Curtain-line reveals that generations of audiences have politely refused to spoil.
Twelve short cases out of the Baker Street rooms: a scandalous photograph, a red-headed clerk, a band of speckled dread. The template every detective story since has been politely stealing from.

titleAtDraft: The Girl Who Played with Fire
new: Three bodies, a magazine investigation into trafficking about to go to print, and a hunted young hacker the whole of Sweden has decided is guilty. Second in the trilogy, and it runs harder than the first.
Winter at a smugglers' inn should be quiet, but guests keep arriving, small things keep vanishing, and the innkeepers' son teams up with a stranger to work out which of the stories are true.

Everyone back home is certain Lucy killed her best friend. Lucy cannot remember that night at all, and now a true crime podcaster has arrived to dig the whole thing up. Wry, mean, very hard to put down.
Everything says the beloved coach murdered a child, and everything says he was somewhere else entirely. Both sets of evidence hold up. Procedural at first, then quietly, horribly frightening.
In postwar Barcelona a boy adopts a forgotten novel and finds that someone has been burning every copy of its author's work. A labyrinth of bookshops, ruined mansions, old cruelties and first love.

Her husband is shot dead, and the painter who did it never speaks again. Years into her confinement a psychotherapist talks his way onto the ward, certain he can reach her. Clean, cold, engineered to blindside you.

titleAtDraft: The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
new: Respectable London hides plenty, and a lawyer pulling at a friend's strange will finds a brutish young man who stands to benefit from it. Slim, feverish horror about what the decent self keeps in the cellar.
Sixteen tenants of a new apartment tower are named heirs to a millionaire's fortune, paired off at random and handed clues that make no sense alone. A puzzle that plays completely fair. Bring paper!

titleAtDraft: The Unexpected Mrs. Pollifax; Mrs. Pollifax #1
new: A New Jersey widow bored with her garden club volunteers as a spy, and to everyone's alarm the agency says yes. The simple errand abroad goes wrong at once: charming, dated and thoroughly game.
An assassin with expensive taste and no conscience, and the intelligence officer who starts noticing a pattern nobody above her will admit exists. Lean, cold chase fiction, opening a short series.
Boston has a killer copying a dead man's methods, and the surgeon who survived the original is the one person who understands what is coming. Clinical, bloody, and the start of a long partnership.

Returning to the pit village he swore never to see again, a teacher takes the only job going, in the place where his sister vanished as a child and came home not quite herself. Bleak and brilliantly creepy.
Retired and happiest in his armchair, a private investigator is hauled off by his globe-trotting bodyguard daughter-in-law, and the bodies and the money follow. Warm, quick and extremely quotable.
One Alabama spring a milk round ends with a car sinking into a bottomless lake and a murdered man strapped inside. A long, magic-soaked memory of boyhood where wonder and horror share a street.

titleAtDraft: The Bullet That Missed; A Thursday Murder Club Mystery #3
new: Four pensioners from a retirement village cannot let go of a cold case out of local television, a body never found and a fortune unaccounted for. Third outing for the club, and one of them is being blackmailed.

titleAtDraft: Escape from Mr. Lemoncello's Library; Mr. Lemoncello's Library #1
new: Twelve lucky kids win a lock-in at the most extravagant library ever built, then learn the only way out is hidden somewhere in the shelves. Puzzles, games and book jokes at sprinting speed.

Two girls, two eras, one shuttered children's home. A diary tells one half and wordless drawings tell the other, closing in on what happened behind those gates. Illustrated, spare and genuinely eerie.

titleAtDraft: Three Bags Full; Sheep Detective Story #1
new: George the shepherd is found dead in his own meadow, so his flock sets out to investigate, led by the cleverest sheep in Ireland. Sheep logic applied to human wickedness, and far funnier than it sounds.
Two patients, one surgeon, a single choice, and a lifetime spent paying for it. Cold adult suspense in comic form, set in Germany, opening a series that turns very, very dark.
